title: One Server, One Night

post.author: u/box_office_hester
post.title: I sell tickets at a small-town picture palace. At midnight, 1,200 requests a second knocked on our website's only door, and most of them got a note from a man who died in 2016.

blocks.text: I run the box office at the Fallow Creek Palace: 1,100 seats, one ticket window, and a website that sells about forty tickets on a good week. In March, Odile Marsh, who last sang on our stage in 1987, said she would sing here once more. One night only. Tickets on sale Friday at midnight.

The website runs on one server, the computer that hands our pages to anyone who asks. We rent it from Kestrel Hosting. It's a virtual machine: a slice of a bigger computer that behaves like a whole one. My nephew Nils looks after it. Every time a phone asks for a page, that's a request. Nils explained the server's capacity to me: the most requests it can finish in a second. Ours is Kestrel's small size. It has two CPU cores, the parts that do the actual work, and costs $0.10 an hour. It finishes about 150 requests a second. Requests that arrive faster wait in a line that holds 900. When the line is full, the server turns new ones away with a 503, the code that means "too busy, come back later."

This is Nils's dashboard, his screen of live numbers, from that night. At 11:59 PM, fans were already refreshing and waiting. Each line shows the time, requests arriving each second, requests that got a page, requests that got a 503, and the p95 wait: 95 of every 100 visitors who got a page waited that long or less. A ms is a thousandth of a second.

23:59:00  arriving 40/s     served 40/s     503s 0/s      p95 68 ms
00:00:00  doors open
00:00:30  arriving 1200/s   served 150/s    503s 1050/s   p95 6000 ms
00:03:00  resizing to x-large (16 cores): server stopped
00:04:30  arriving 1200/s   served 0/s      no answer 1200/s
00:06:00  server started: x-large, $0.80/h
00:06:30  arriving 1200/s   served 1000/s   503s 200/s    p95 900 ms

So the lucky ones who got a page waited six seconds. Everyone else got our 503 page at once, and nobody had read it in years. Abel, our old projectionist, wrote it in 2004, when he built our first website. He died in 2016. *The house is full. Please wait in the lobby. I'll find you a seat.*

At three minutes past, Nils switched the server to Kestrel's biggest size. To resize, Kestrel stops the server, moves it to a bigger machine and starts it again. For three minutes nothing answered at all, and Kestrel's graph kept counting knocks on a door that wasn't there. When it opened, the biggest machine Kestrel rents still turned away 200 requests a second, at eight times the price.
One machine. One door. And we had closed it ourselves.
We sold out at 12:41 AM. On Saturday Nils measured every size Kestrel rents:

blocks.title: KESTREL HOSTING, server sizes
items: small: 2 cores, finishes 150 requests a second, $0.10 an hour
medium: 4 cores, 290 a second, $0.20 an hour
large: 8 cores, 560 a second, $0.40 an hour
x-large: 16 cores, 1,000 a second, $0.80 an hour. The biggest Kestrel rents.

blocks.text: Odile has added a second night, next Friday at midnight. Nils says there's no bigger server to buy. What do we do?

blocks.label: dashboard_0000.png

diagram.aria: Nils's dashboard at 00:00:30 on Friday. 1,200 requests a second from fans reach the Palace's only server, a small size that can finish 150 a second, whose waiting line of 900 is full. 150 a second get a page after about 6 seconds. 1,050 a second are turned away with a 503 and Abel's lobby page.

blocks.caption: Nils redrew his dashboard from 00:00:30 for me. 1,200 requests a second met a server that finishes 150. Those 150 got a page after about six seconds in line. The other 1,050, every second, got Abel's lobby page at once.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Every server has a capacity, and past it the only choices are a line or a no. Nils tried making the one machine bigger. Engineers call that vertical scaling. But one machine is a single point of failure: one part whose failure takes everything down. The other way is horizontal scaling: more machines of the same size. In front of them sits a load balancer, a machine that spreads visitors across the servers, like a host seating diners at different tables. How many small ones would 1,200 a second need? Now, how many would you actually run?

replies.author: u/box_office_hester
replies.text: Nils says eight. Then he said ten, and wouldn't tell me why until I'd guessed.

comments.author: u/two_racks_ronan
comments.text: Before you add machines, check one thing: can any of them answer any fan? Say a fan is halfway through an order. If your site keeps that in one server's memory, its short-term working space, the next click may land on a different server that has never heard of them. Keep it in the database instead. That's the site's filing cabinet of records, outside the servers, where every server can see it. A new server takes about two minutes to start: it switches on, loads the site, then joins the load balancer's list. So start them before the doors open, not at midnight. And put them in two zones. Availability zones are separate buildings with their own power, so one power cut can't take every server at once.

comments.author: u/queued_since_midnight
comments.text: I got the lobby page fourteen times. Big ticket sites put you in a waiting room: a page that lets fans in a few at a time and shows your place in line. Here you just knock until the door opens. On the fifteenth refresh I waited six seconds and got two tickets. My grandmother was at Odile's show in 1987. She says that night Abel stood at the door and told the line outside: the house is full, wait in the lobby, I'll find you a seat.

reply.prompt: Odile's second night goes on sale next Friday at midnight. Nils has a week. What should he do? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the server at Kestrel's biggest size from now on, so nobody has to resize it at midnight and the site never goes dark.
options.verdict: Trade-off: fewer failures, still one door
options.part2: Nils left it at the biggest size. On Friday at midnight 1,200 requests a second arrived again. The server finished 1,000 and turned 200 away every second, so Abel's page went out until we sold out at 12:39. Then the bill came: $0.80 an hour, every hour of the month, for a site that sells forty tickets on a good week. On Sunday at 3 AM Kestrel restarted the machine for maintenance, and for four minutes the Palace didn't exist.
options.senior: A bigger machine lifts capacity, but only up to the biggest size anyone rents. You pay its price every hour, even on quiet nights. And it's still one machine: one restart, crash or resize and the whole site is gone.

options.text: Make the waiting line much longer, say 20,000 places, so every fan at midnight gets a place and nobody sees the 503 page.
options.part2: Nils made the line hold 20,000. At midnight nobody saw Abel's page. The pages just spun. With 20,000 in line and 150 finished a second, the newest fan would wait over two minutes, and fans gave up or refreshed long before that. The server didn't know. It kept working through the line, building ticket pages for people who had already gone. At 12:20 Nils watched it finish page after page for nobody.
options.senior: A longer line adds waiting, not capacity. Past a few seconds people give up or refresh, and the server spends its work on requests nobody is waiting for. A quick 503 is kinder than two minutes of a spinning wheel.

options.text: Keep one small server, with a waiting room page in front that lets fans in 150 a second and shows the rest their place.
options.part2: Nils added the waiting room. Nobody saw Abel's page. Fans waited their turn, the line moved at exactly 150 a second, and we weren't going to sell out until after 1 AM. At 12:58 Kestrel restarted the server for an urgent repair. The waiting room lived on the same server, and two thousand fans lost their place in line at once. When it came back, they all pressed refresh together.
options.senior: A waiting room is a real tool, and big ticket sites use one. But it adds no capacity: it only makes the line orderly. On one machine it's still one door, and when that machine stops, the line goes with it.

options.text: Ten small servers behind a load balancer in two zones, started before midnight, each 80% busy, orders in the database.
options.part2: Nils started ten small servers at 11:30, five in each of two zones, behind Kestrel's load balancer. At midnight 1,200 requests a second arrived, 120 for each server, and 95 of every 100 fans got a page within a quarter of a second. At 12:14 one server's disk failed. For two minutes, until Nils took it out of the list, a tenth of the fans got nothing, because the load balancer didn't know. The other nine carried on. We sold out at 12:37, and at 1 AM he shrank back to two. The ten cost $1.00 an hour. Nobody has seen Abel's page since, except Nils, at 3:12 this morning: one request for a single ticket, from the old kiosk in the lobby that Abel set up. Nobody knew it was still plugged in.
options.senior: Use many small, identical servers behind a load balancer. Capacity grows by adding machines. Losing one costs a slice instead of everything. And you pay for the extras only on the night. It works only if any server can answer any fan, and only if the servers are running before the crowd arrives.

sim.title: Open the doors at midnight
sim.lede: You're Nils at 11:59 PM. The dots are a sample of the requests fans send to the Palace's website, and the numbers below count all of them, per second. Every server has a capacity. Past it, requests wait in the server's line, which holds 900, and when the line is full they get 503. The p95 wait is a teaching model: an idle server answers in 50 ms, the wait climbs as a server fills up, and past capacity it's the time to get through a full line. The clock runs 20 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Doors open and watch one small server finish 150 requests a second while 1,050 get 503. Change the size to x-large, Kestrel's biggest: three minutes of nothing, then 1,000 a second served and 200 still turned away, for $0.80 an hour. Reset, press Doors open, and add servers one at a time. Each takes two minutes to start, and you pay for it from the moment you add it. Eight small servers also cost $0.80 an hour and keep up, but at 100% busy the wait hits 6,000 ms. Ten bring it down to 250 ms for $1.00 an hour. Pull the plug on one of the ten, then remove it. Last, reset and pull the plug on the only server. A pulled plug stays pulled until you remove that server or reset.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the website. 1,200 requests a second reached one server that could finish 150, so the rest were turned away. The only fix at hand, a bigger machine, shut the only door for three minutes and still came up short.

steps.title: Capacity is a number: requests per second.
steps.text: A server finishes requests at a certain rate. That rate is its capacity. It depends on its CPU cores (the parts that do the work), its memory (its short-term working space) and how much work each page takes. Kestrel's small size finishes 150 a second. Below capacity, every request gets a page. But waits still climb as the server fills up. Fans arrive in bursts, so someone is always just behind someone else. That's why engineers watch p95, short for the 95th percentile: the wait that 95 of every 100 requests stay within. The average would hide the people at the back of the line. The sim's numbers are a teaching model, a simplified sum that shows the shape of real behavior. An idle small server answers in 50 ms, thousandths of a second. At 80% busy the p95 is 250 ms, and near 100% it shoots up.

steps.title: Past capacity: a line, then 503s.
steps.text: When requests arrive faster than they finish, the extra ones wait in a line. Engineers call it a queue. At midnight it grew by 1,050 every second, so its 900 places filled in under a second. From then on the server took 150 a second from the line. Each one had waited about six seconds (900 divided by 150). The other 1,050 got 503 Service Unavailable, the too-busy code, at once. A longer line adds waiting, not capacity. Past a few seconds, most people give up or press refresh, which sends yet another request. Apps, and proxies (middlemen that pass requests along), may give up too: they hit a timeout, a limit on how long they'll wait. Meanwhile the server goes on working through requests nobody is waiting for.

steps.title: Vertical scaling: a bigger machine.
steps.text: Scaling up means moving to a bigger server with more cores and memory. Nothing in the code changes, and there's still one machine to look after. That's why it's often the first thing teams try. It has three catches. First, a ceiling: every host has a biggest size. Kestrel's tops out at 16 cores and 1,000 requests a second. Second, a cost curve, the way the price grows as you climb. Kestrel's price doubles with every size, but the site didn't get twice as fast each time. Some of its work can only happen one step at a time, and extra cores can't speed that part up. So each extra request a second costs more as you climb, and you pay the big price every hour, busy or not. Third, downtime, time when nothing answers at all, because a resize usually happens in three steps. First the host stops the server, and every request in its line is lost. Then it moves the server onto a bigger machine, and nothing answers while it moves. Then it starts the server again, which takes a while, and if the start fails, the site stays dark. On AWS, Amazon's cloud, a rented virtual machine is called an instance, and its size is its instance type. You must stop an instance before you can change its instance type.

steps.title: Horizontal scaling: more machines.
steps.text: Scaling out means adding more servers of the same size, with a load balancer in front to spread visitors across them. Capacity grows machine by machine. Eight small servers cost the same $0.80 an hour as one x-large, and finish 1,200 a second instead of 1,000. Ten finish 1,500, so 1,200 keeps each one 80% busy, with room for a bad minute. You start them before the rush, because starting takes about two minutes in three steps. First the machine switches on; if the host is short of machines, this can fail. Then the site's program loads; a bad setting can stop it here. Then the load balancer adds it to its list; until then it gets no visitors. You remove them after, so you pay for the extras only on the night. It asks one thing of the code: every server must be able to answer every visitor. So nothing a visitor needs may live only in one server's memory. A server that keeps nothing about a visitor between requests is called a stateless server. This season's next two cases cover the load balancer and that rule.

steps.title: One machine was a single point of failure.
steps.text: A single point of failure is one part whose failure takes the whole system down. The Palace's one server was one. A crash, a restart or a resize, and the site was gone. That's exactly what happened at three minutes past midnight. With ten servers, losing one costs a tenth of the capacity. The other nine carry the load if there's room to spare. Now spread them across two availability zones, separate buildings with their own power and network. Losing a whole zone then costs half, not everything. The parts every server shares, like the database, still need the same question asked of them.

diagram.aria: The fix for the second night. 1,200 requests a second from fans reach a load balancer, which spreads them over ten small servers, five in availability zone AZ-a and five in AZ-b, 600 a second to each zone. Each server gets 120 a second and is 80% busy, with a p95 wait of 250 ms. All ten use one shared database that holds orders and sign-ins, so any server can answer any fan.

notes.text: any server can answer any fan

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the second night. Ten small servers, five in each of two availability zones, sit behind a load balancer. It spreads 1,200 requests a second over all of them: 120 each. So every server is 80% busy, with room to spare. Any server can answer any fan, because orders and sign-ins live in the shared database, not in one server's memory. Lose one server and the other nine carry on.

fix.title: The fix: scale out, with room to spare, before the doors open
fix.text: Estimate the peak, the busiest moment, in requests a second: 1,200. Divide by what one server can finish: 150. Then add room to spare, so each server sits well below 100% at the peak and losing one doesn't overload the rest. That gives ten small servers, not eight. First make them interchangeable, able to stand in for each other: anything a visitor needs between requests lives in the shared database, not in one server's memory. Put a load balancer in front. Spread the servers across at least two availability zones. Start them well before midnight. A day early, send them a planned rush, called a load test, to check the numbers. After the sale, scale in, which means removing servers, down to two, never one. Keep vertical scaling for parts that can't be split easily yet, like the database, and do that resize at a quiet hour.

limits: More servers move the limit; they don't remove it. Every server still uses the same database. So a shared part becomes the next ceiling and the next single point of failure: the database, the load balancer itself, or the network. Later cases take them one at a time.

This case's load balancer is simple. It doesn't notice a dead server, and keeps sending it its share until someone removes it. How a load balancer chooses a server, and checks that it's alive, is the next case.

Adding servers takes minutes, and most automatic scaling reacts after the fact. New servers need time to start. On AWS, an Auto Scaling group keeps a set of servers running and can add more. Its target tracking policy works like a thermostat: it adds servers only once a measure, such as average CPU use, has passed its target. Predictive scaling can start them early, but only for daily or weekly patterns it has already seen. For a one-off rush at a known minute, add them ahead of time with scheduled scaling, a change set for a fixed time. And none of it works until the servers are interchangeable, which takes work in the code.

head: What matters
Vertical: a bigger server
Horizontal: more servers
rows: Up to the biggest size sold. Kestrel's stops at 16 cores and 1,000 requests a second.
As far as you keep adding servers, until something they share, like the database, becomes the limit.
The price per request a second usually climbs as you go up. A program rarely gets twice as fast on twice the cores. And you pay it every hour, even on quiet nights.
Each server costs the same, and you pay for the extras only while they run.
Usually a stop and start: three minutes of nothing at the Palace.
Add servers while the others keep serving. Each takes a couple of minutes to start.
Everything stops. It's a single point of failure.
You lose a slice. The rest carry on if they have room to spare.
What it asks of the code
Nothing. The same program on a bigger machine.
Any server must be able to answer any visitor, and you need a load balancer in front.

explain.seniorTake: Scale up until it hurts, then scale out. A bigger machine is the simplest fix, and often the right first step, especially for a database. But it has a ceiling, a climbing price and a single door. Many small, interchangeable servers behind a load balancer grow as far as the parts they share allow. Losing one of them is a bad minute instead of a dark site. Either way, know your capacity in requests a second before the crowd arrives, and keep room to spare.

realWorld.title: Ticketmaster and the Eras Tour presale, November 2022
realWorld.text: On November 19, 2022, Ticketmaster, a large ticket-selling company, published its own explanation of the November 15 presale for Taylor Swift's Eras Tour. A presale is an early sale for people with a code. Over 3.5 million people had signed up in advance through its Verified Fan program, which it called the largest registration in history. Around 1.5 million were sent codes to join the sale, and the other 2 million were put on a waiting list. On the day, it wrote, a staggering number of bot attacks drove unprecedented traffic, along with fans who didn't have codes. Bots are programs that use a site automatically, often to grab tickets for resale. Its systems got 3.5 billion requests in total, 4 times its previous peak. It estimated that about 15% of interactions across the site had problems. Some were errors checking passcodes, which made fans lose tickets in their carts. It slowed down some sales and pushed back others to steady its systems. It still sold over 2 million tickets that day, the most ever sold for an artist in a single day. The post doesn't say how Ticketmaster's systems are built. So the lesson here is the arithmetic: a peak four times the biggest you have seen will find the limit of whatever you planned for.

realWorld.title: HealthCare.gov, October 2013
realWorld.text: HealthCare.gov is the US government's website for buying health insurance. In a February 2016 case study, the Office of Inspector General, the independent watchdog of the US Department of Health and Human Services, described its launch. On September 26, 2013, four and a half days before launch, some limited performance testing, which measures how much load a site can take, gave a warning. The site could support far fewer concurrent users, people using it at the same moment, than planned. Part of the reason was that its software needed more computing capacity than CMS had expected. CMS, short for Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, was the agency running it. CMS asked its hosting contractor to double the capacity within 72 hours, and the contractor added more than double. On October 1 the site had 250,000 concurrent users, much more than its planned capacity. Outages began within 2 hours of launch. Only six people managed to submit an application and choose a plan that first day. The report notes that the US Chief Technology Officer, the government's head of technology, blamed the volume: five times the simultaneous users expected. But the site also had core problems in its own performance. After weeks of repairs it could handle more than 35,000 concurrent users without crashing. When it was overloaded, it held visitors in waiting rooms until traffic fell.

realWorld.title: AWS's own design principles
realWorld.text: AWS's Well-Architected Framework is its published guide to designing systems on AWS. Among its design principles for reliability, it lists "scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability". A workload is AWS's word for the set of machines and code that does one job. The idea: replace one large machine with several small ones, so a single failure hurts less, and spread requests across them so they don't share one point of failure. The next principle is "stop guessing capacity". It names resource saturation, when demand is more than the capacity, as a common cause of failure for systems run in a company's own building. It suggests watching demand and adding or removing machines automatically, while noting that there are still limits.

realWorld.title: What a resize costs on AWS
realWorld.text: EC2 is AWS's service for renting virtual machines, called instances. Its guide says you must stop an instance before you can change its instance type, its size. It tells you to plan for downtime while it's stopped. Stopping it and changing the type might take a few minutes, and starting it again takes a variable amount of time. It starts again on new hardware. It may also get a new public IP address, its number on the internet. AWS keeps the old number only if it's an Elastic IP address, a fixed one you rent separately. Otherwise anything that found the server by its old number, such as a DNS record in the internet's phone book, has to catch up.

realWorld.title: How big one general-purpose machine gets on AWS
realWorld.text: AWS sells its instances in families of sizes. Its general-purpose M7i family runs from m7i.large up to m7i.48xlarge. The smallest has 2 vCPUs, AWS's unit of CPU power, and 8 GiB of memory (a GiB is a little over a billion bytes). The biggest has 192 vCPUs and 768 GiB. That ceiling is far higher than Kestrel's, but it is still a ceiling. A workload that outgrows the biggest machine has to be split across several. Other families go bigger, but every family has a top size.

asked: Your URL shortener's redirect traffic just went up tenfold. How do you scale it?
Vertical or horizontal scaling: what are the trade-offs, and when would you pick each?
interview.answer: Start with numbers: the peak in requests a second, and what one server can handle, measured, not guessed. Then name both directions. Scaling up means a bigger machine. It needs no code changes, but it has a ceiling, a price that climbs, a resize that usually means downtime, and it's still a single point of failure. Scaling out means more identical servers behind a load balancer. It grows much further and survives losing one. But every server must be able to answer every request, so nothing about a user may live only in one server's memory. A URL shortener turns long web addresses into short links. Its redirect, the answer that sends a visitor on to the long address, only looks up a short code. So once the codes live in a shared store outside the servers, any server can answer any redirect. Scale the redirect servers out. Run enough for the peak, with room to spare, across at least two availability zones, and add them before a known spike. Then say what becomes the limit next: the shared store and the load balancer, which the rest of this season covers.

terms.def: The most requests a second a server, or a set of servers, can finish. Past it, the extra requests wait in line or are turned away.
How many requests arrive, or are finished, each second, written req/s or /s. The usual way to measure a site's traffic and a server's capacity.
The busiest moment, usually measured in requests a second. You size servers for the peak, not the average.
A sudden jump in traffic, like the minute tickets go on sale.
Spare capacity kept on purpose, so a bigger rush or a lost server doesn't push the rest past 100%. Also called room to spare.
A waiting line. Requests that have arrived but not been started wait in it, first come, first served. The Palace's server's line held 900.
The 95th percentile: 95 of every 100 requests took this long or less. Engineers watch it because an average hides the slow ones at the back of the line.
A cut-off point in a set of measurements. If the 95th percentile wait is 250 ms, then 95 of every 100 requests waited 250 ms or less.
A simplified calculation that shows the shape of real behavior, not exact real-world numbers. The sim's p95 wait is one.
Making one server bigger: more CPU cores and memory. Also called scaling up. Simple, but it has a ceiling, the price climbs, and resizing usually means stopping the server.
To scale vertically: move to a bigger machine.
Adding more servers of the same kind and spreading the work across them. Also called scaling out. Needs a load balancer and servers that can each answer any visitor.
To scale horizontally: add more machines.
To remove servers you no longer need, for example after a rush, so you stop paying for them.
A machine that spreads visitors across several servers so no one server gets them all, like a host seating diners. The next case shows how it chooses a server and notices a dead one.
One part whose failure takes the whole system down, like a website's only server. Two or more copies, spread out, remove it.
Changing a server to a bigger or smaller size. On most hosts, AWS included, the server is stopped, moved to other hardware and started again, so it is down for minutes.
Time when a system doesn't answer at all.

How the price of each extra request a second changes as you grow. On one ever-bigger machine it usually climbs, because the program speeds up less than the cores grow. With more same-size machines it stays flat.
A page that holds visitors when a site is busy and lets them in a few at a time, often showing their place in line. It adds no capacity.
Able to stand in for each other. Servers are interchangeable when any of them can answer any visitor's next request.
A server that keeps nothing about a visitor between requests, so any copy can answer the next one. Case 3 of this season covers it.
A place outside the servers, such as a database, where data lives so that every server can read it.
Sending a planned amount of traffic at a system on purpose, before the real crowd arrives, to measure how much it can take.
Measuring how fast a system answers and how much load it takes before it struggles. A load test is one kind.
People using a site at the same moment. HealthCare.gov's launch capacity was planned and measured this way.
A large company that sells tickets for concerts, sports and shows.
A ticket sale before the general sale, open only to people with a code or a membership.
Ticketmaster's presale sign-up: fans register in advance, and some are sent codes that let them join the sale.
A program that uses websites automatically. Ticket bots try to grab tickets faster than people can, often to resell them.
On a shopping site, the things you've picked but not paid for yet.
The US government's website for buying health insurance, launched on October 1, 2013.
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the US government agency that ran HealthCare.gov.
The independent watchdog office inside a US government department. The one at Health and Human Services wrote the HealthCare.gov case study.
The person in charge of technology for an organization. The US government has one too.
AWS's published guide to designing systems that are reliable, secure, efficient and affordable. It is grouped into themes, called pillars, such as reliability.
AWS's word for the resources and code that together deliver one thing, like the Palace's ticket site.
When the demand on a system is more than its capacity. AWS lists it as a common cause of failure.
The size and kind of an EC2 instance, a rented AWS virtual machine, like m7i.large or m7i.48xlarge. It sets the CPU power, the memory and the price.

Virtual CPU: the unit of CPU power AWS sells. On M7i and most other Intel types, one vCPU is one of a core's two threads, its lanes of work. On newer AMD types such as M7a, and on Graviton, it is a whole core.
Gibibyte: 1,073,741,824 bytes, a little more than a gigabyte. AWS states memory in GiB.
A family of general-purpose EC2 instance types, from m7i.large (2 vCPUs, 8 GiB of memory) to m7i.48xlarge (192 vCPUs, 768 GiB).
A fixed internet address (IPv4, the common kind) that you rent from AWS and attach to an instance, so the address stays the same when the instance is stopped and started.
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: the AWS service that keeps a chosen number of instances running and adds or removes instances as load changes.
A set of EC2 instances that AWS keeps at a chosen number, between a minimum and a maximum, replacing unhealthy ones and adding or removing instances as load changes.
How many instances an Auto Scaling group should be running right now. You set it, or a scaling policy changes it.
A rule that tells an Auto Scaling group when to add or remove instances.
A scaling policy that keeps a measure, like average CPU, near a target value, adding instances above it and removing them below, the way a thermostat holds a temperature.
Changing an Auto Scaling group's size at a set time, like an hour before tickets go on sale.
An AWS Auto Scaling policy that forecasts load from the daily and weekly patterns it has seen, and starts servers before the rise it expects.
A service that turns a long web address into a short link and sends anyone who opens the link to the long address. It is this season's finale interview.
An answer telling the web browser to go to another address instead, like a forwarding note. One kind is 301 Moved Permanently, with the new address in its Location header.

atWork: Open the EC2 console, AWS's control screen for rented servers, in your team's production account, the one real customers use. Read-only access is enough. Pick one web service. How many instances (rented virtual machines) run it, and of which instance type, or size? If it's one instance, that's a single point of failure, and growing it means stopping it. If it's an Auto Scaling group, a set AWS keeps at a chosen size, open the group. Read its minimum, maximum and desired capacity, the number it aims to run right now. Read what its scaling policy, its rule for adding servers, tracks. That's often average CPU use against a target. Check whether any scheduled actions add instances before known busy times. Then find the service's capacity. Use a load test if your team has one. If not, use the requests a second its load balancer counted at the busiest hour last month, and the CPU use that took. Write down what happens if traffic triples at a known minute: how long a resize would keep it down, how long new instances take to start, and who would press the button.

recall.prompt: Your company's checkout, the page where shoppers pay, runs on one EC2 instance, a rented AWS server. On a normal afternoon its CPU is 85% busy. Marketing has a sale next Thursday at 10 AM that should triple the traffic. Your manager says: we'll just switch it to a bigger instance type, a bigger size, that morning. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Changing the instance type means stopping it: downtime, on sale day
Bigger has a ceiling and a price, and it's still one machine: a single point of failure
Scale out instead: several instances behind a load balancer, started before 10 AM, with room to spare
Check the instances are interchangeable: nothing about a shopper kept in one server's memory

recall.model: Not that morning, and probably not only bigger. Changing an EC2 instance type means stopping the instance, so checkout would be down for minutes on sale day. At 85% CPU today, three times the traffic is about 2.5 times what this instance can do. So we'd need a much bigger type, at a higher price every hour, and it would still be one machine: if it fails, checkout is gone. I'd run several instances behind a load balancer, across two availability zones. I'd run enough that each stays well below 100% at the sale's peak, and start them before 10 AM, for example with a scheduled change to an Auto Scaling group. First I'd check that nothing about a shopper lives only in one server's memory, so any instance can serve any request. Then I'd load test it this week.

recall.prompt: One small server can finish 150 requests a second, and its waiting line holds 900. At midnight 1,200 a second arrive. Once the line is full, what happens each second?
options: All 1,200 get a page, each a little slower
About 150 get a page after waiting about six seconds, and about 1,050 get 503 at once
The server speeds up to keep pace
recall.why: Capacity doesn't stretch. The server keeps finishing 150 a second from its line, each after waiting 900 divided by 150, six seconds, and with the line full, the other 1,050 are turned away straight away.

recall.prompt: Nils resizes the Palace's only server to Kestrel's biggest size in the middle of the rush. What happens first?
options: Nothing answers at all for about three minutes, because a resize stops the server
Capacity rises at once, with no interruption
The waiting line doubles in size
Fans are moved to a second server automatically
recall.why: A resize usually means stopping the machine, moving it to bigger hardware and starting it again. With only one server, the whole site is down until it's back, which is why a single server is a single point of failure.

recall.prompt: Before you add more servers behind a load balancer, what must be true of them?
options: They must all be the biggest size available
They must each have their own database
They must all sit in the same availability zone
Any of them must be able to answer any visitor, so nothing a visitor needs lives only in one server's memory
recall.why: The load balancer may send a visitor's next request to a different server. If that server can't see what the first one stored, the visitor is a stranger to it. Interchangeable servers are what make adding more work.

recall.prompt: A teammate plans next month's launch: the peak will be 1,200 requests a second, each server can finish 150, so they'll run exactly 8. What's missing from that plan?

keyIdeas.idea: At 100% busy, waits shoot up: plan room to spare, each server well below 100%
If one server fails, the other seven are overloaded: add at least one extra
Estimates can be wrong and the real peak higher: measure and load test
Start them before the peak, across zones

recall.model: Eight servers at 150 each is exactly 1,200, so at the peak every one of them is 100% busy. Waits shoot up long before that, and the first burst above the estimate turns into 503s. If one server fails, the other seven can finish only 1,050, so 150 a second are turned away. Run ten or more, so each sits around 80% at the peak and losing one still leaves room. Spread them across two availability zones and start them before the peak. And load test at the expected rate, because the real peak is often higher than the guess.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Nils moved the site to a load balancer and two small servers, rising to ten on on-sale nights. Then the Palace started selling memberships. Fans sign in, and their basket, the seats they've picked but not paid for yet, is kept in the memory of whichever server they signed in on. At Friday's sale the servers coped fine: every fan got a page within a quarter of a second. But all night fans found their baskets empty and were asked to sign in again, sometimes twice in a minute. Nils wants to go back to one huge server, "so everyone lands in the same place".
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's going wrong, and is one huge server the fix?

keyIdeas.idea: The load balancer sends each request to any server, and the basket lives only in one server's memory
Make the servers interchangeable: keep sign-ins and baskets in a shared store such as the database
One huge server brings back the ceiling, the cost and the single point of failure

coldCase.model: Nothing is wrong with the servers' capacity. The load balancer spreads requests across all ten. So a fan's next click usually lands on a different server, and that server's memory has never heard of their basket or their sign-in. One huge server would hide that by putting everyone in one place. But it brings back everything from the first night: a biggest size it can't grow past, a price paid every hour, and one machine whose restart or resize takes the whole site down. Keep the ten servers and make them interchangeable instead. Store sign-ins and baskets in the shared database, or a store built for sessions, so any server can answer any fan. That's the subject of this season's third case.
